examples.problem_statement: Etienne began to eat 20 cookies at exactly the same time Jacques began making more cookies, one at a time, at a constant rate of 16 cookies per hour. If Etienne ate 20 cookies per hour, after how many hours were there no cookies?

solution.operation: \text{eating rate opposes making rate} \Rightarrow \text{subtract, not add}
solution.description: Recognise that Etienne and Jacques work at cross-purposes: one destroys cookies while the other creates them. Work rates are usually added, but when one party gains on another -- just like a car chase -- the rates are subtracted instead.
Subtract the making rate from the eating rate to get the net rate, so the size of the cookie pile decreases by 4 cookies every hour.
Divide the starting pile of 20 cookies by the net decrease of 4 cookies per hour to find how long the pile lasts before it reaches zero.

key_reminders: Add work rates when parties help each other; subtract them when one undoes the other's work.
A net-rate problem reduces to time = starting quantity / net rate.
The net rate must stay positive for the pile to run out -- here the eater outpaces the baker.
common_mistakes: Adding 20 + 16 = 36 cookies/hour and getting 20/36 of an hour instead of subtracting the opposing rates.
Assuming Etienne only ever ate the initial 20 cookies; over 5 hours he actually ate 100 -- the original 20 plus the 80 Jacques baked.

concept.technique_name: sum and product of roots of a quadratic

examples.problem_statement: Two numbers a and b are such that the quadratic equation ax^2 + 3x + 2b = 0 has -6 as the sum and the product of the roots. Find a + b. Options: (a) 2, (b) -1, (c) 1, (d) -2

solution.description: Set the sum of the roots of ax^2 + 3x + 2b = 0, which equals -3/a, equal to the given value -6.
Solve that equation for a, which gives a equal to one half.
Set the product of the roots, 2b/a, equal to -6 and substitute the value of a just found to solve for b.
Add the two values found for a and b to produce the quantity the question asks for.

key_reminders: For ax^2 + bx + c = 0 the sum of the roots is -b/a and the product is c/a.
Here b = 3 and c = 2b of the problem, so the sum is -3/a and the product is 2b/a.
Both conditions must be used: the sum fixes a, and only then can the product fix b.
common_mistakes: Confusing the problem's constant 2b with the standard formula's coefficient b and writing the sum of roots as -2b/a.
Dropping the minus sign and solving 3/a = -6, which flips the sign of a and hence of b.

concept.sub_category: Ratio and Proportion -- time and work efficiency

examples.problem_statement: A can do a piece of work in 12 days. B is 60% more efficient than A. Find the number of days it takes B to do the same piece of work.

solution.description: Write the efficiency ratio by taking A's efficiency as 100 and adding the 60% by which B is more efficient, giving B an efficiency of 160.
Invert the efficiency ratio to get the ratio of days, because days taken vary inversely with efficiency, then reduce 160 : 100 to 8 : 5.
Scale A's actual 12 days through the days ratio: divide 12 by A's ratio part 8 to get one part, then multiply by B's ratio part 5.
Check with the rule of fraction: since B is the more efficient worker, multiply A's 12 days by the fraction 100/(100+60), which is less than 1, and get the same result.

key_reminders: Days taken are inversely proportional to efficiency, so the days ratio is the efficiency ratio reversed.
'60% more efficient' means efficiency 160 against a base of 100, not 60.
Rule of fraction: the more efficient worker must take fewer days, so the multiplying fraction 100/160 has to be less than 1.
common_mistakes: Using the efficiency ratio directly for days and computing 12 x 160/100 = 19.2 days, making the faster worker slower.
Reading '60% more efficient' as an efficiency of 60 and multiplying by 60/100.

concept.technique_name: division by a fraction as multiplication by its reciprocal

examples.problem_statement: Simplify, applying BODMAS and remembering that each \times or \div sign applies only to the number immediately following it: \frac{4}{5} \div \frac{7}{12} \times \frac{5}{24}

solution.description: Replace the division by 7/12 with multiplication by its reciprocal 12/7, so the whole expression becomes a single chain of multiplications.
Multiply the three fractions and cancel common factors across numerators and denominators to reduce the product to its simplest form.

key_reminders: Dividing by a fraction is the same as multiplying by its reciprocal.
A division or multiplication sign applies only to the number immediately following it, so the reciprocal is taken of 7/12 alone.
Multiplication and division are carried out before addition and subtraction under BODMAS.
common_mistakes: Taking the reciprocal of the wrong term -- flipping 5/24 or 4/5 instead of the divisor 7/12.
Working right to left and computing 7/12 x 5/24 first, then dividing 4/5 by that product.
